newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bond yields bumped up at close in budget's wake.
newsitem.headline: NZ bond yields bumped up at close in budget's wake.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (SEP) 93.05 (PREV 93.07) 90-DAYS 7.02 (PREV 6.97)
OVERNIGHT CASH 6.50 PCT (PREV 6.50) US 5-YR 6.34 (PREV 6.33)
RBNZ MCI NZ/MCI 824 (PREV 813) NZ MCI -1.03 (PREV -1.15)

New Zealand bond yields sold off a touch in the wake of the coalition government's first budget on Thursday, but the market's underlying tone remained strong ahead of Friday's key statement from the central bank.
The 02/01 and 11/06 maturities both ended three basis points higher in yield, at 6.85 and 7.04 percent respectively. Volumes were fairly light.
The markets were surprised by very little in the budget, as lower operating surpluses and a higher bond programme were well flagged by Treasurer Winston Peters last week.

Dealers said some of their number had hoped Peters was getting the bad news out of the way last week, clearing the path for some pleasant surprises in the budget. None eventuated, however, prompting some of the optimists to square up their positions.
"But there's ongoing support, and every time the market backs up there is continued support," a Wellington dealer said.
"There is not a huge amount of supply around locally."

The government's projected surplus for 1997/98 fell to NZ$1.5 billion, from $3.3 billion projected in the March Budget Policy Statement (BPS). The projected surpluses for 1998/99 and 1999/00 were also lower.
The country's economic growth rate was seen peaking at 4.2 percent in the year to March 1999. GDP growth for 1997/98 was projected at 2.4 percent, against the March BPS forecast of 3.6 percent.

The Debt Management Office (DMO) announced a 1997/98 bond tender programme worth NZ$1.8 billion in total, including $300 million inflation-indexed bonds. Forecasts for the size of the programme had ranged from $1.2 billion to around $2 billion.
Bond dealers welcomed news that the DMO would launch a new 10-year benchmark bond, maturing on July 15, 2009.
Meanwhile, the short end of New Zealand's yield curve also finished weaker on Thursday ahead of Friday's key Monetary Policy Statement (MPS) from the Reserve Bank.
The 90-day bank bills ended five pips higher in yield at 7.02 percent, while the September futures contract was two weaker at 93.05.
Dealers said the market had priced in reasonably good news from the MPS. Many felt the economy was not as buoyant as the Treasury's short term growth forecasts suggested.
"If the RBNZ back that up, then short term that's probably quite positive for inflation," one dealer said.

He commented that if the RBNZ took a conservative stance over the appropriate degree of monetary easing and economic indicators continued to be soft, the market could well decide the RBNZ had got it wrong and continue to push conditions below the levels desired by the bank.
-- Catherine McCaw, Wellington newsroom (64 4) 471 4275
